parts.name: Q1 (compulsory)
parts.sweep: Short answers from across the syllabus. Read the key points and formulas of every topic once — 30 minutes is enough.

pattern.summary: Q1 is compulsory (10 marks of short maths answers + 10 marks of short statistics answers). Then answer 2 of 4 questions from Part A (Maths) and 2 of 4 from Part B (Statistics). Each question carries 20 marks. A simple, non-scientific calculator is allowed.
pattern.note: Before June 2022 the paper had no compulsory question: 2 of 4 questions from each part, 25 marks each.

sessionNotes.2020-12: Held in February 2021 (COVID). Old pattern: 2 of 4 questions per part, 25 marks each.
sessionNotes.2021-12: Old pattern: 2 of 4 questions per part, 25 marks each.

choosing: Q1 is compulsory: learn one-line definitions and formulas from every topic — matrix types, SI/CI formulas, quartiles, index number, time-series components.
Part A: Differentiation ('find dy/dx, any four') and Compound Interest appear almost every session and are pure method — the safest picks.
Part B: Index Numbers (Fisher's index and its tests) and Time Series (least squares trend, components) are asked every session.
Pick numericals you can finish. A fully worked problem scores more reliably than a long theory answer in this paper.
numerical: Write the formula first, then substitute, then the answer with units (₹, years, %). Formula lines earn marks by themselves.
Show the working table (x, y, x², xy …) for correlation, regression, SD and trend questions — examiners mark the table.
For 'any four' dy/dx questions, attempt exactly four and name the rule used (product, quotient, chain).
Round only at the last step; keep 2–4 decimals in between.

topics.name: Differentiation (dy/dx)
topics.summary: Usually 'find dy/dx, any four' for 20 marks — pure practice, very predictable.
points: Derivative dy/dx = rate of change of y with respect to x.
Standard results: d/dx(xⁿ) = n·xⁿ⁻¹; d/dx(constant) = 0; d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ; d/dx(log x) = 1/x; d/dx(aˣ) = aˣ·log a.
Implicit functions (e.g. x² + y² = 25): differentiate both sides, collect dy/dx terms.
Parametric (x = at², y = 2at): dy/dx = (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt).
Function of a function (y = u³, u = 3x + 9): chain rule dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.
method: Identify the form: sum, product, quotient, chain, implicit or parametric.
Write the rule you are using as the first line.
Differentiate each part, then simplify.
For xˣ type: take log on both sides, then differentiate (logarithmic differentiation).
mistakes: Wrong sign order in the quotient rule (it is v·u′ − u·v′).
Forgetting to multiply by du/dx in the chain rule.

topics.name: Simple & Compound Interest
topics.summary: Asked every session: CI numericals (varying rates, half-yearly, doubling time) or theory on SI vs CI, present value, nominal vs effective rate.
points: Simple interest: interest only on the principal. Compound interest: interest on principal plus accumulated interest.
Nominal rate: stated annual rate. Effective rate: actual annual rate when interest compounds more than once a year.
Present value: today's value of a future sum, found by discounting.
Discount factor = 1 / (1 + r)ⁿ.
Equation of value: equates the values of two sets of payments at one date.
method: Write P, R, T (and n compounding periods per year).
Half-yearly: rate ÷ 2, periods × 2. Monthly: rate ÷ 12, periods × 12.
Different rates each year: A = P(1 + r₁)(1 + r₂)(1 + r₃).
Doubling time: 2 = (1 + r)ⁿ → n = log 2 ÷ log(1 + r).
CI = A − P.
mistakes: Not adjusting the rate and periods for half-yearly or monthly compounding.
Giving the amount when the question asks for compound interest.

topics.name: Maxima, Minima & Applications of Derivatives
topics.summary: Local maxima/minima, increasing/decreasing intervals, marginal revenue and elasticity.
points: Increasing where f′(x) > 0, decreasing where f′(x) < 0.
Stationary points where f′(x) = 0.
Second derivative test: f″(x) < 0 → local maximum; f″(x) > 0 → local minimum.
Marginal revenue MR = d(TR)/dx; marginal cost MC = d(TC)/dx; profit is maximum where MR = MC.
Price elasticity of demand = (% change in quantity) ÷ (% change in price); income elasticity uses income; cross elasticity uses the price of another good.
method: Find f′(x) and set it to 0; solve for x.
Find f″(x) and check its sign at each x.
Put each x back into f(x) to get the maximum or minimum value.
For intervals: factor f′(x), mark the roots on a number line, test signs.
mistakes: Stopping at f′(x) = 0 without the second-derivative test.
Not stating the maximum or minimum value itself.

topics.name: Functions in Business (Cost, Revenue, Profit)
topics.summary: Cost, revenue, profit and demand functions, break-even, and composite/inverse functions (f∘g, g∘f).
points: Function: a rule giving exactly one output for each input.
Types: linear (y = a + bx), quadratic, absolute value |x|, step function, exponential.
Cost function C(x) = fixed cost + variable cost × x. Average cost = C(x)/x.
Revenue function R(x) = price × x. Profit P(x) = R(x) − C(x).
Demand function: quantity demanded as a function of price.
Composite function: (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)). Inverse function: reverses f, exists when f is one-to-one.
method: Break-even: set R(x) = C(x) and solve for x.
f∘g: substitute g(x) wherever x appears in f.
g∘f: substitute f(x) into g — usually a different answer.
formula: BEP (units) = Fixed cost ÷ (Selling price − Variable cost per unit)
mistakes: Mixing up the order in f∘g and g∘f.

topics.name: Inverse Matrix, Cramer's Rule & Equations
topics.summary: Solve 2 or 3 equations by Cramer's rule or the matrix (inverse) method, or find an inverse.
points: A system AX = B has solution X = A⁻¹B when |A| ≠ 0.
Inverse exists only for a square matrix with non-zero determinant.
Properties: (A⁻¹)⁻¹ = A; (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹; (Aᵀ)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)ᵀ; AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I.
method: Cramer's rule: find D = |A|. Replace column 1 by constants → D₁; column 2 → D₂; column 3 → D₃.
x = D₁/D, y = D₂/D, z = D₃/D.
Inverse method: find |A|, the cofactor matrix, adjoint (transpose of cofactors), then A⁻¹ = adj A ÷ |A|.
Check: substitute the answers back into one equation.
mistakes: Forgetting the sign pattern (+ − +) for cofactors.
Not transposing the cofactor matrix to get the adjoint.

topics.name: Matrices & Determinants
topics.summary: Types of matrices (often in Q1), operations, determinants and their properties, business uses.
points: Matrix: a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns; order m × n.
Types: row, column, square, rectangular, diagonal, scalar, identity/unit, zero, symmetric, skew-symmetric, orthogonal (AAᵀ = I), transpose.
Equal matrices: same order and equal corresponding elements.
Multiplication AB is possible when columns of A = rows of B; AB ≠ BA in general; (AB)C = A(BC); A(B + C) = AB + AC.
Determinant properties: interchanging rows changes the sign; two identical rows → 0; |Aᵀ| = |A|; a common factor can be taken out.
Business uses: storing sales/production data, costing orders (quantity × price), solving equations, input–output analysis.
method: Construct aᵢⱼ matrix: substitute each i (row) and j (column) in the given rule.
Bill/production problems: write quantities as one matrix, prices as another, multiply.

topics.name: Input–Output Analysis
topics.summary: An occasional 20-mark theory question on Leontief's input–output model.
points: Developed by Wassily Leontief: shows how the output of one industry is an input to others.
Transaction table: rows show how each sector's output is used; columns show the inputs each sector uses.
Technology (input) coefficient aᵢⱼ = input from sector i per unit output of sector j.
Output needed: X = (I − A)⁻¹ D, where D is final demand.
Hawkins–Simon conditions ensure the system is workable.
Uses: economic planning, forecasting sector output, finding the effect of demand changes.
topics.frame: Meaning and origin → assumptions → transaction table with a small 2-sector example → the formula X = (I − A)⁻¹D → uses and limitations.

topics.name: Limits & Continuity
topics.summary: Occasional: evaluate limits (factorisation, rationalisation) or find points of discontinuity.
points: lim x→a f(x) is the value f(x) approaches as x gets close to a.
0/0 form: factorise and cancel, or rationalise, then substitute.
Continuity at a: f(a) exists, the limit exists and equals f(a).
Standard limits: lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n·aⁿ⁻¹; lim (eˣ − 1)/x = 1 as x → 0.
method: Substitute first. If you get 0/0, factorise or rationalise, cancel, substitute again.
formula: lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n·aⁿ⁻¹ as x → a

topics.name: Index Numbers
topics.summary: Every session: Fisher's ideal index with time and factor reversal tests, or theory on types, tests and construction problems.
points: Index number: measures relative change in price, quantity or value compared with a base year.
Types: price, quantity, value; simple and weighted (Laspeyres, Paasche, Fisher).
Problems in construction: purpose, choice of base year, selection of items, price quotations, choice of average, weights, formula.
Tests: unit test, time reversal test (P₀₁ × P₁₀ = 1), factor reversal test (P₀₁ × Q₀₁ = Σp₁q₁/Σp₀q₀), circular test.
Fisher's index satisfies both time reversal and factor reversal tests — hence 'ideal'.
method: Make a table: p₀q₀, p₁q₀, p₀q₁, p₁q₁ for each item; total each column.
Laspeyres = Σp₁q₀/Σp₀q₀ × 100; Paasche = Σp₁q₁/Σp₀q₁ × 100.
Fisher = √(L × P).
Expenditure given instead of quantity: q = expenditure ÷ price.
mistakes: Multiplying by 100 before checking the reversal tests (tests use ratios without ×100).

topics.name: Time Series
topics.summary: Every session: components/utility theory, or fitting a straight-line trend by least squares.
points: Time series: data arranged in order of time.
Components: secular trend, seasonal variation, cyclical variation, irregular variation.
Models: additive Y = T + S + C + I; multiplicative Y = T × S × C × I.
Trend methods: freehand, semi-averages, moving averages, least squares.
Utility: understand past behaviour, forecast, compare, plan business activity.
Preliminary adjustments: calendar days, population, price changes, comparability of data.
method: Take X = year − middle year (odd number of years) so ΣX = 0.
a = ΣY / n, b = ΣXY / ΣX².
Trend Yc = a + bX for each year.
Forecast: put the X of the required year into Yc = a + bX.
mistakes: Using the actual year instead of the deviation X.
Wrong X for the forecast year.

topics.name: Measures of Dispersion
topics.summary: Standard deviation, variance, quartile deviation, mean deviation and combined SD.
points: Dispersion: how spread out values are around the average.
Absolute measures (range, QD, MD, SD) are in original units; relative measures (coefficients, CV) are pure numbers for comparison.
Coefficient of variation CV = SD/Mean × 100 — lower CV means more consistent.
Quartile deviation = (Q₃ − Q₁)/2.
method: Grouped SD (step deviation): d = (x − A)/i; SD = i × √[Σfd²/N − (Σfd/N)²].
Quartiles: Q₁ at N/4 item, Q₃ at 3N/4 item, then L + (pos − cf)/f × i.
Combined mean = (N₁x̄₁ + N₂x̄₂)/(N₁ + N₂); combined SD uses dᵢ = x̄ᵢ − x̄₁₂.
mistakes: Forgetting to multiply by the class width i in step deviation.
Using cumulative frequency of the quartile class instead of the class before it.

topics.name: Meaning, Functions & Limitations of Statistics
topics.summary: Theory for Q1(b) or a full 20-mark Part B question.
points: Statistics (plural): numerical data; (singular): methods of collecting, organising, analysing and interpreting data.
Functions: simplifies complex data, enables comparison, helps forecasting, tests hypotheses, helps policy making.
Importance in business: market research, quality control, forecasting sales, financial analysis, auditing (sampling).
Limitations: studies aggregates not individuals, only quantitative facts, results true on average only, can be misused.
Descriptive statistics summarise data; inferential statistics draw conclusions about a population from a sample.
topics.frame: Definition (both senses) → 6–8 headed points → one business example each → conclusion.

topics.name: Measures of Central Tendency
topics.summary: Mean, median, mode calculations and theory on merits, demerits and requisites of a good average.
points: Measures: arithmetic mean, median, mode, geometric mean, harmonic mean, weighted mean.
Requisites of a good average: rigidly defined, easy to understand, based on all items, capable of algebraic treatment, least affected by sampling and extreme values.
AM ≥ GM ≥ HM for positive values.
Empirical relation: Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean.
method: Mean (grouped): x̄ = A + (Σfd/N) × i.
Median: find N/2 in the cf column → L + (N/2 − cf)/f × i.
Mode: modal class (highest f) → L + (f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂) × i.
'Less than' cumulative data: convert to class frequencies first.
formula: Mode = L + (f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂) × i
mistakes: Using the cf of the median class instead of the class before it.

topics.name: Regression
topics.summary: Regression equations/coefficients by least squares, and theory on properties of regression coefficients.
points: Regression estimates the value of one variable from another.
Two lines: Y on X (estimate Y) and X on Y (estimate X); both pass through (x̄, ȳ).
Properties: r = ±√(bᵧₓ × bₓᵧ); both coefficients have the same sign; if one is > 1 the other is < 1; independent of change of origin but not of scale.
method: Table: x, y, x², y², xy (or deviations from the means).
bᵧₓ = [nΣxy − ΣxΣy]/[nΣx² − (Σx)²]; bₓᵧ = [nΣxy − ΣxΣy]/[nΣy² − (Σy)²].
Y on X: y − ȳ = bᵧₓ(x − x̄). X on Y: x − x̄ = bₓᵧ(y − ȳ).
mistakes: Giving r a sign different from the coefficients.

topics.name: Correlation
topics.summary: Karl Pearson's or Spearman's rank correlation numericals, and correlation vs regression theory.
points: Correlation measures the degree and direction of relationship between two variables; r lies between −1 and +1.
Positive (move together), negative (move opposite), zero (no linear relation).
r is unaffected by change of origin and scale (only sign may change with a negative scale).
Correlation vs regression: degree of relationship vs estimating one variable; r symmetric vs two different lines; no cause-effect vs dependent/independent variables.
method: Karl Pearson: table of x, y, dx, dy, dx², dy², dxdy; r = Σdxdy / √(Σdx² × Σdy²) (deviations from actual means).
Spearman: rank both series, D = R₁ − R₂, ρ = 1 − 6ΣD²/[n(n² − 1)].
mistakes: Ranking in opposite orders for the two series.
